question: In the lecture, the derivative of \(f(x)=\alpha x^n\) was shown to exist at every point \(c\) in an interval \(I\). Explain how the definition of derivative leads to the formula \(f'(c)=n\,\alpha\,c^{\,n-1}\) and why this holds regardless of whether \(I\) is open, closed, or unbounded.
answer:
The derivative at a point \(c\) is defined as the limit
\[
 f'(c)=\lim_{x	o c} rac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c}\,.
\]
For \(f(x)=\alpha x^n\) we compute the difference quotient:
\[
 rac{\alpha x^n-\alpha c^n}{x-c}=\alpha\, rac{x^n-c^n}{x-c}\,.
\]
Using the factorisation \(x^n-c^n=(x-c)(x^{n-1}+x^{n-2}c+\dots+xc^{n-2}+c^{n-1})\), the quotient simplifies to
\[
\alpha igl(x^{n-1}+x^{n-2}c+\dots+xc^{n-2}+c^{n-1} igr).
\]
Taking the limit as \(x	o c\) replaces each \(x\) in the sum by \(c\), yielding
\[
\alpha igl(n\,c^{\,n-1} igr)=n\,\alpha\,c^{\,n-1}.
\]
Thus the limit exists for every real \(c\), so \(f\) is differentiable at every point of any interval \(I\subset\mathbb{R}\), whether \(I\) is open, closed, or unbounded. The polynomial \(f\) is continuous everywhere, and the algebraic simplification shows the limit is independent of the interval’s endpoints, guaranteeing differentiability throughout \(I\).
